# RQ2 - Immune-related signatures

Are 18-gene T-cell–inflamed GEP (see D6; Ayers et al. (2017)) **associated** with treatment response?

Reference: 10.1172/JCI91190 (18 genes)

**Suggested tasks:**

-   **Q2.1:** Identify the 18 genes included in the published T-cell–inflamed GEP (gene expression profile) and examine their expression in the dataset.

-   **Q2.2:** Calculate a T-cell–inflamed GEP score for each patient.

-   **Q2.3**: Investigate whether patients with higher GEP scores are more likely to respond to anti-PD-L1 treatment.

-   **Q2.4:** Interpret the biological significance of your findings and discuss why a high T- cell–inflamed GEP score does not necessarily guarantee treatment response.

## Setup and inspection of datasets

```{r}
# Loading packages
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ggplot2)
  library(pheatmap)
})

# Load datasets
counts <- readRDS("../data/counts.rds")
tpm <- readRDS("../data/tpm.rds")
clinical <- readRDS("../data/clinical.rds")

# Dimensions
print(list(
  counts = dim(counts),
  tpm = dim(tpm),
  clinical = dim(clinical)
))

# align tpm to clinical table
clinical <- clinical[clinical$BOR %in% c("NR", "R"), ]
stopifnot(all(clinical$sample_id %in% colnames(tpm)))

# reorder tpm matrix columns to match with clinical table
tpm <-  tpm[
  , match(clinical$sample_id, colnames(tpm)),
  drop = FALSE
]

# verify output order
stopifnot(
  identical(as.character(clinical$sample_id), colnames(tpm))
)
```

Dim() outputs \[rows, columns\], in our case \[genes, samples\], which follows good practice for expression datasets.

\
The counts and tpm matrices consist of 31087 genes and 192 patient samples.\
The clinical matrix consist of 192 patient samples and 4 clinical variables.

TPM expression data is aligned to the clinical data, to ensure it contains the samples in correct order - to avoid incorrect GEP scoring –\> patient matching

## Q2.1: Identify the 18 genes included in the published T-cell–inflamed GEP (gene expression profile) and examine their expression in the dataset.

```{r}
# STEP 1: create extended panel (including gene PDCD1 from week 6 exercise)
GEP_genes <- c("TIGIT", "CD27", "CD8A", "PDCD1LG2", "LAG3", "CD274", "CXCR6", "CMKLR1", "NKG7", "CCL5", "PSMB10", "IDO1", "CXCL9", "HLA-DQA1", "CD276", "STAT1", "HLA-DRB1", "HLA-E", "PDCD1")

# checking we have 19 genes
length(GEP_genes)

# assessing dataset genes
all_genes <- rownames(tpm)

# checking gene name format
head(all_genes)

# checking presence
GEP_genes_present <- GEP_genes[GEP_genes %in% rownames(tpm)]
GEP_genes_missing <- setdiff(GEP_genes, rownames(tpm))

cat("GEP genes present:", length(GEP_genes_present), "of", length(GEP_genes), "\n")
cat("Missing genes:", paste(GEP_genes_missing, collapse = ", "), "\n")



# STEP 2: Checking GEP_genes are present in dataset
GEP_genes %in% rownames(tpm)
GEP_genes[GEP_genes %in% rownames(tpm)]



# STEP 3: Extract + logtransform g.expression (tpm)
# IMPORTANT TO LOG TRANSFORM (visualization + scoring)
GEP_expression <- log2(tpm[GEP_genes, , drop = FALSE] +1 )
dim(GEP_expression) # 192 patients



#STEP 4: Checking expression
# per gene
summary(t(GEP_expression))

# median expression per gene
apply(GEP_expression, 1, median)

# checking low counts (how many patients have an expression value = 0, per gene)
rowSums(GEP_expression == 0)

# inspecting HLA-DQA1 low gene counts (TPM)
# extract tpm for HLA-DQA1 + log transformed expression + add BOR
HLA_DQA1 <-  data.frame(
  TPM = as.numeric(tpm["HLA-DQA1", ]),
  GEP_expression = as.numeric(GEP_expression["HLA-DQA1", ]),
  BOR = clinical$BOR
)

# nr of patients with zero expression in each response group
with(HLA_DQA1, table(BOR, zero_exression = GEP_expression == 0))

# count patients in each response group
table(clinical$BOR, useNA = "ifany")

# percantage
with(
  HLA_DQA1, 
  tapply(GEP_expression == 0, BOR, function(x) mean(x) * 100)
)
```

Checking the gene name format to ensure same format is used (dataset vs subset of T cell inflammed genes)

\
Most genes are expressed in most patients, except HLA-DQA1.\
HLA-DQA1 has a TPM expression of 0 in 129 out of 192 samples, specifically:

-   113 out of 167 NR patients, corresponding to \~68%

-   16 out of 25 R patients, corresponding to 64%\

```{r}
# STEP 5: Visualize - expression heatmap
annotation <- data.frame(Response = clinical$BOR,
                         row.names = clinical$sample_id)

ord <- order(clinical$BOR)

pheatmap(GEP_expression[, ord, drop = FALSE],
         #standardize each gene ACROSS patients
         scale = "row",
         annotation_col = annotation[ord, , drop = FALSE],
         cluster_cols = FALSE,
         show_colnames = FALSE,
         main = "GEP gene expression according to response group"
         )


# checking correlation between genes using spearman
# checking GEP gene expressioin has valid sd first (> 0)
gene_sd <- apply(GEP_expression, 1, sd)

stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(gene_sd)),
  all(gene_sd > 0)
)

# transpose (genes = cols, patients = observations)
gene_cor <- cor(
  t(GEP_expression),
  method = "spearman"
  )

pheatmap(
  gene_cor, 
  main = "Spearman correlation between GEP genes",
  breaks = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 101),
  color = colorRampPalette(c("blue", "white", "red"))(100)
)
```

Heatmap:

-   Used to suggest patterns

GEP_expression heatmap:

-   Each row = gene and each column = patient

-   Colors represent the gene wise z scores across patients (and not absolut TPM values)

-   Tree = hierchal clustering (based on genes with sim patterns)

-   Patients ordered by response group

Gene-gene spearman correlation heatmap:

-   Rows + cols = genes

<!-- -->

-   Correlation coefficients describe the gene-gene patterns (+/- = direction, size = strength), but not statistical significance or treatment response

-   Positive correlation = patients with higher expression of gene X tend to have higher expression of gene Y

-   Negative correlation = patients with higher expression of gene X tend to have lower expression of gene Y

-   The correlation does not = similar absolute expression values

-   Dendogram = group genes with similar correlation profiles

## **Q2.2:** Calculate a T-cell–inflamed GEP score for each patient.

-   Standardize each gene across patients (avoid dominating genes)

-   Average across the 19 genes per patient (1 nr per patient –\> if high =\> more inflamed compared to other patients)

```{r}
# STEP 1: confirming data
dim(GEP_expression)

stopifnot(
  identical(
    colnames(GEP_expression),
                    as.character(clinical$sample_id)))



# STEP 2: Check no gene is constant (0 var cant be standardized)
gene_sd <- apply(GEP_expression, 1, sd)
gene_sd
any(gene_sd == 0)
```

No constant genes –\> continue to standardization

Scale = standardize cols (have to transpose t(), as genes are rows)

Transpose gene expression –\> scale –\> transpose back again (genes = rows)

```{r}
# STEP 3: Standardize across patients
GEP_scaled <- t(scale(t(GEP_expression)))

# checking standarzation 
round(rowMeans(GEP_scaled), 10) # mean of 0
apply(GEP_scaled, 1, sd) # sd of 1



# STEP 4: Average standardized expression ACROSS the gene subset
GEP_scores <- colMeans(GEP_scaled)

length(GEP_scores)
summary(GEP_scores)



# STEP 5: add clinical data (building data frame)
df <- data.frame(
  sample_id = clinical$sample_id,
  BOR = factor(clinical$BOR, levels = c("NR", "R")),
  GEP_score = GEP_scores
)

# numeric coding (required for spearman response analysis)
# responders = 1, non responders = 0
df$Response_binary <- as.integer(df$BOR == "R")

# safety check --> confirm scores matches correct patients
stopifnot(
  identical(
    df$sample_id, names(GEP_scores)),
  all(is.finite(df$GEP_score))
  )

head(df)
table(df$BOR, useNA = "ifany") #add NA column if any present


# STEP 6: visualize
hist(
  df$GEP_score,
  breaks = 20,
  main = "GEP_score distribution",
  xlab = "Mean standardized expression of the 19 genes"
  )

# summary per response group
tapply(df$GEP_score, df$BOR, median)
```

GEP score (cohort relative, not universally true)

-   Positive score = indicative of a higher average standardized expression (relative to this cohort)

-   Negative score = indicative of a lower average standardized expression (relative to this cohort)

Summary per response group:

-   Responders have a higher median T cell inflammed GEP score (\~0.676), compared to patients with progressive disease (\~-0.096)

-   Could indicate a more active T cell inflammation profile in responders

## **Q2.3**: Investigate whether patients with higher GEP scores are more likely to respond to anti-PD-L1 treatment.

AKA is the score associated with the treatment response?

= Compare GEP score to response group

Our df is defined with NR as reference group

Wilcon rank sum test = compare 2 independent groups (without assuming normal distr.) (rec week6)

-   0 hyp: scores in the 2 groups come from the same distribution

```{r}
# group comparison from w6 exercises
# reusing df from 2.2

# STEP 1: Test difference between NR and R groups (wilcoxon rank sum test)
GEP_response_test <- wilcox.test(
  GEP_score ~ BOR,
  data = df,
  exact = FALSE)

GEP_response_test



# STEP 2: Plot difference
# helper function from w6 ex (advanced)
plot_Response_boxplot <- function(data, variable, y_label, test_result) {

  # keep the groups in order
  data$BOR <- factor(data$BOR, levels = c("NR", "R"))

  # descriptive response labels with patient counts
  n_per_group <- table(data$BOR)

  group_labels <- c(
    NR = paste0(
      "Progressive disease (NR)\nn = ",
      n_per_group["NR"]
    ),
    R = paste0(
      "Complete response (R)\nn = ",
      n_per_group["R"]
    )
  )

  # red = NR; blue = R
  group_colours <- c(
    NR = "#D9534F",
    R = "#2E86C1"
  )

  ggplot(
    data,
    aes(
      x = BOR,
      y = .data[[variable]],
      fill = BOR,
      colour = BOR
    )
  ) +
    geom_hline(
      yintercept = 0,
      linetype = "dashed",
      colour = "grey60"
    ) +
    geom_boxplot(
      outlier.shape = NA,
      alpha = 0.25,
      width = 0.5
    ) +
    geom_jitter(
      width = 0.12,
      height = 0,
      alpha = 0.7,
      size = 2
    ) +
    annotate(
      "text",
      x = Inf,
      y = Inf,
      label = paste0(
        "Wilcoxon p = ",
        signif(test_result$p.value, 3)
      ),
      hjust = 1.1,
      vjust = 1.5,
      colour = "black"
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = group_colours) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = group_colours) +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = group_labels) +
    labs(
      title = "T-cell–inflamed GEP score by treatment response",
      subtitle = paste0(
        "Each dot is one patient; ",
        "dashed line = cohort average (score 0)"
      ),
      x = NULL,
      y = y_label
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
}

# creating the plot
plot_Response_boxplot(
  data = df,
  variable = "GEP_score",
  y_label = "T-cell inflamed GEP score (mean z-score of the 19 genes)",
  test_result = GEP_response_test
)


# STEP 3: Spearman correlation with binary response
# response is R = 1 and NR = 0
GEP_response_cor <- cor.test(
  x = df$GEP_score,
  y = df$Response_binary,
  method = "spearman",
  exact = FALSE
)

GEP_response_cor

# Compact results table
response_results <- data.frame(
  n_NR = sum(df$BOR == "NR"),
  n_R = sum(df$BOR == "R"),
  median_NR = median(df$GEP_score[df$BOR == "NR"]),
  median_R = median(df$GEP_score[df$BOR == "R"]),
  Spearman_rho = unname(GEP_response_cor$estimate),
  Spearman_p = GEP_response_cor$p.value,
  Wilcoxon_p = GEP_response_test$p.value
)

response_results
```

-   Positive spearman coefficient is indicative of responders having higher GEP score ranks, compared to non-responders

-   Spearman does not estimate response probability or odds ratio

-   Spearman and Wilcoxon analyze rank based associations in the same patient cohort - they dont validate each other

-   Notice the R group size is smaller than NR

## **Q2.4:** Interpret the biological significance of your findings and discuss why a high T- cell–inflamed GEP score does not necessarily guarantee treatment response.

Assessing; direction of association, group distributions, spearman coefficient and p values together

The gene panel is indicative of a T cell inflamed tumor environment (abundance of immune cells, inerferon related signaling, antigen presentation and inhibitory immune regulation)

A high score is not = a guaranteed treatment response.

Bulk RNA expression doesnt infer the spatial location of immune cells or whether immune cell reach the tumor cells OR if other tumor resistance mechanisms prevent effective killing of these

Observed associations/patterns within the cohort has been analyzed. No validated predictor or any individual response can be obtained from this.

The analysis hasnt adjusted for any possible confounders (eg tumor purity, see Q4)

**Conclusions:**

-   Responders had a higher observed T-cell–inflamed GEP score on average

**Cannot conclude:**

-   Score value indicates response

-   Score dictates which patient will respond to treatment

-   If the score would be similar in another cohort
